title: Moses Almost Missed It Before Egypt
paragraphs:
Moses Almost Missed It Before Egypt
The Forgotten Night That Nearly Ended Israel's Deliverer Before His Calling Ever Began
History remembers the plagues.
It remembers the Red Sea splitting apart.
It remembers Pharaoh's army drowning beneath walls of water.
It remembers Mount Sinai shaking beneath the glory of God.
It remembers the Ten Commandments.
But almost no one remembers the night Moses nearly died before he ever stepped into Egypt.
One quiet, mysterious, unsettling passage of Scripture almost erased the greatest deliverer of the Old Testament before his ministry ever truly began.
No battle.
No Pharaoh.
No Egyptian soldier.
No political enemy.
No demon is mentioned.
Only God.
The very God who had just called Moses through the burning bush suddenly confronted him on the journey and sought to put him to death.
That single sentence has caused confusion for generations.
How could the God who had just chosen Moses suddenly seek to kill him?
The answer is not found by reading casually.
It is found by slowing down.
By entering the covenant.
By seeing Scripture through the eyes of its original audience.
And once you understand what happened that night, you may discover that this ancient story is not primarily about Moses at all.
It is about us.
It is about what happens when God calls someone into great ministry while hidden disobedience remains buried beneath public obedience.
It is about the scandal that grace refuses to ignore.
Because before God changes nations...
He changes hearts.
Before He confronts Pharaoh...
He confronts His servant.
Before public miracles...
there is private surrender.
That pattern has never changed.
The account appears in Exodus 4:24–26, one of the most mysterious passages in all of Scripture:

"At a lodging place on the way, the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, 'Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!' So He let him alone." (ESV)
At first glance, almost every question seems unanswered.
Why was God angry?
Why now?
Why circumcision?
Why did Zipporah act instead of Moses?
Why does everything suddenly stop after one act of obedience?
To understand this moment, we must go back nearly five centuries before Moses was born.
God had entered into a covenant with Abraham.
In Genesis 17, the Lord declared:

"וְאַתָּה אֶת־בְּרִיתִי תִשְׁמֹר"
(Ve'attah et-beriti tishmor.)
"And as for you, you shall keep My covenant."
Then came the covenant sign:

"וּנְמַלְתֶּם אֵת בְּשַׂר עָרְלַתְכֶם"
(Unemaltem et-besar orlatkhem.)
"You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin."

Circumcision was never intended as a magical ritual or merely an ethnic tradition. It was the visible sign that a family belonged to the covenant promises of God. Every male descendant was to bear this mark as an outward testimony of an inward relationship established by God's grace.
The Hebrew word for covenant is בְּרִית (berit), a binding covenant relationship established by God Himself. It carried obligations because covenant love always produces covenant faithfulness.
God was not demanding perfection.
He was requiring obedience born from trust.
The covenant was never earned.
But it was never meant to be ignored.
Moses knew this.
Raised as a Hebrew by his own mother before entering Pharaoh's palace, he would have known the story of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. He knew what circumcision meant.
Yet somewhere during forty years in Midian, something had happened.
Perhaps fear.
Perhaps compromise.
Perhaps tension within his marriage.
Perhaps simply delay that turned into neglect.
Scripture does not tell us why.
It simply tells us that one of his sons remained uncircumcised.
That hidden act of disobedience stood directly against the covenant God had already established.
The Hebrew text says:

"וַיִּפְגְּשֵׁהוּ יְהוָה"
(Vayyifgeshehu YHWH.)
"The LORD encountered him."
The verb פָּגַשׁ (pagash) is not casual. It often describes an overwhelming encounter, one that cannot be escaped. God was not merely visiting Moses. He was confronting him.
The issue was not that Moses had failed once.
The issue was that he was preparing to represent the holy God before kings while quietly neglecting obedience within his own household.
God's messenger cannot ignore the covenant while announcing it to others.
Leadership begins long before public ministry.

The Apostle Paul would later echo this principle when describing spiritual leadership. A man who cannot faithfully lead his own household is not prepared to shepherd God's people (1 Timothy 3:4–5). Though Paul writes in a different covenantal context under Christ, the underlying principle remains consistent: private faithfulness matters.
The pattern is striking throughout Scripture.
Noah built before the flood.
Abraham obeyed before Isaac.
Joseph endured before Pharaoh.
David faced lions before Goliath.
The apostles were formed before Pentecost.
Even our Lord Jesus Christ spent years in quiet obedience before His public ministry began.

He is the perfect fulfillment of covenant faithfulness. Unlike every servant before Him, Jesus never failed in obedience. Where Adam fell, where Israel wandered, and where Moses stumbled, Christ remained perfectly faithful.
The New Testament uses the Greek word διαθήκη (diathēkē) for "covenant." Jesus declared at the Last Supper:

"Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη..."
(Touto to potērion hē kainē diathēkē...)
"This cup is the new covenant..." (Luke 22:20)
The New Covenant does not abolish God's holiness.
It reveals how God's holiness and mercy meet perfectly in Jesus Christ.
That is why Exodus 4 is not a story about legalism.
It is a story about covenant faithfulness.
Moses could not proclaim God's authority while resisting God's command.
And neither can we.
How often do we ask God to bless what we refuse to surrender?
How often do we pray for influence while quietly protecting areas of compromise?
How often do we ask God to open doors while leaving unfinished obedience behind us?
Before Egypt...
God dealt with Moses.
Before ministry...
God addressed the man.
Before miracles...
God exposed the hidden place.
That is still His way.

Perhaps this is why this forgotten passage feels so uncomfortable. We would rather imagine that God overlooks private compromise because our public intentions seem sincere. Yet Scripture repeatedly shows that the Lord cares as deeply about the unseen life as the visible one. His correction is not cruelty. It is covenant love refusing to leave His servant unchanged.
That is where the Gospel begins to shine.
Because every scandal God exposes is one He intends to redeem.
Every hidden wound He uncovers is one He desires to heal.
Every act of repentance becomes another testimony that grace is greater than our failures.
Moses almost missed Egypt.
Peter almost missed restoration.
Paul almost missed Damascus.
You and I have our own moments where hidden compromise threatens the very calling God has prepared for us.

Yet the same God who confronted Moses is the God who, in Christ, extends mercy to all who repent and believe. Jesus bore the covenant curse we deserved so that all who trust Him might receive the covenant blessing by grace through faith (Galatians 3:13–14). Salvation is never earned by our obedience; it is the gift of God. But genuine saving faith produces a transformed life that increasingly delights to obey the One who first loved us.
If this message has challenged your heart and strengthened your faith, would you prayerfully help us spread God's truth?
Your testimony may encourage another believer to step into repentance, healing, and renewed obedience.
Sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God opens the sea—but that He first opens our hearts.
